title: The Potluck by César Alvarez presented by Soho Rep and Intar Theatre ...
transcript: This new musical is a beautiful mess that throws everything at you but the kitchen sink. Five revolutionaries in the Communist Workers’ Party fell victim to a state-sanctioned massacre in Greensboro, North Carolina in 1979, shortly after which a survivor gave birth to writer and composer César Alvarez. Through a loosely autobiographical account of the creation of this musical and the unpacking of this inherited trauma, César, as the central character, curates a personal and family history, a tribute, and a séance, all in one. Interestingly enough, it opens with a humorously scorching critique of capitalism and a meta commentary on the creation of art itself before getting into the concrete background information. The way the piece ebbs and flows between personal narrative and general musings on life, solidarity and queerness, for example, is at times disjointed, but never frustratingly so. César presents a wide array of threads that make for a nonlinear experience, but an emotionally satisfying one nonetheless. César’s parents become pivotal emotional anchors for the piece in Act 2, making way for a catharsis that you don't even realize you need until it happens. As much as the show is thematically abundant, it is equally sonically sprawling — Between the dramaturgically appropriate use of actor-musicians, the dense orchestrations, and the vocal arrangements that range from ethereal to wall-of-sound, it's a plethora of riches. Soho Rep and Intar are presenting The Potluck at Playwrights Horizons through August 2nd. With that, another program for my collection.
